conventions.convention: SGD uses deterministic positive finite stepsizes, x_t measurable with respect to F_t, and G_t measurable with respect to F_{t+1}. The procedure itself imposes no unbiasedness, variance bound, or independence across iterations.
All minibatch vectors are evaluated at the same current iterate; averaging alone asserts neither independence nor variance reduction.
Conditional expectations are coordinatewise almost-sure classes under AC; vector conditional variance is the sum of coordinate conditional variances.
The random output index is independent of the original trajectory on an explicitly constructed finite probability-space extension.
The weighted output samples indices 1 through N with weights proportional to 2γ_k−Lγ_k², requiring 0<γ_k<2/L. The global infimum is finite but need not be attained.
Empirical-risk sampling is over a fixed ordered sample, independently with replacement within each batch; the example asserts no population-gradient identity.
The noise-floor example uses a separate finite sign space for each horizon, with horizon-consistent moments; its infinite-time limit is a limit of those moments.

load_bearing.statement: For a continuously differentiable function with finite Lipschitz-gradient constant, a finite SGD recursion with finite real stepsizes, square-integrable initial point and square-integrable directions has square-integrable iterates and gradients, and integrable objective values at every time through the horizon.

For each iteration t=1,…,N, query the oracle at x_t and set x_{t+1}=x_t−α_tG_t. Return the trajectory through x_{N+1}; no conditional mean, variance, or independence-across-iterations property is part of the definition.

For any probability space and finite probability vector (p_1,…,p_N), there is an extension carrying an independent index R with P(R=k)=p_k; for integrable real H_1,…,H_N, H_R is integrable and E[H_R]=Σ_k p_k E[H_k].

Under AC, the stated smoothness, square-integrability, positive alignment, conditional-mean norm, conditional-variance and trajectory lower-bound hypotheses give E[T⁻¹Σ_{t=1}^T‖∇f(x_t)‖²] ≤ αLM/μ + 2(f(x_1)−F_inf)/(Tμα) for 0<α≤μ/(LM_G). Positive deterministic steps with divergent sum and square-summable squares give expected stepsize-weighted average stationarity tending to zero.

Under AC, the stated smoothness, finite global infimum, deterministic initialization, square-integrable conditionally unbiased oracle and variance bound σ², steps 0<γ_k<2/L and independent output weights a_k/S_N give L⁻¹E‖∇f(x_R)‖² ≤ (D_f²+σ²Σ_kγ_k²)/Σ_k(2γ_k−Lγ_k²), with the stated constant-step bounds and separate zero cases.

seams_checked.note: Read the prerequisite page and its deterministic stationarity theorem. This is a conceptual prerequisite rather than a direct theorem citation: the SGD proofs use the published smoothness inequality directly. They preserve the distinction between stationarity and iterate or minimizer convergence, and explicitly distinguish trajectory lower bounds from a finite global infimum.

The cited supervised-problem and risk definitions permit arbitrary fixed ordered samples and extended nonnegative risk. The owned empirical quadratic example supplies finite smooth losses and computes the fixed-sample gradient directly. Algorithm remarks correctly require separate justification for a population differentiation-under-expectation identity.

The prerequisite is contextual: the inspected RMSProp, Adam and AMSGrad definitions do not cite an owned SGD theorem or inherit its stationarity guarantee. Their coordinate scaling, momentum, clipping or projection are explicitly specified as distinct procedures.

The convex and nonconvex stability theorems state their own sample-selection recurrences and assumptions. They do not invoke conditional unbiasedness or an owned stationarity theorem; uniform marginal sampling may have cross-time dependence. Both explicitly restrict their generalization claims to the specified sample-selection procedure, consistently with the general SGD interface.
